content:
The dining room of the Hôtel des Bergues smelled of beeswax, old money, and the faint, metallic tang of a Lake Geneva autumn. 

Julian Vane sat across from Arthur Sterling, who was currently mid-sentence in a loud, sweeping anecdote about a failed venture in Macau. Sterling was a man of excessive appetites—excessive volume, excessive jewelry, and an excessive fondness for the hotel’s signature *Consommé Double*.

The waiter, a man named Morel, hovered at the periphery of their vision. He was unnervingly still, his posture too rigid for a seasoned professional. He didn’t so much serve as he did haunt the table, appearing silently behind Sterling just as the man reached for his spoon.

Vane watched Morel’s hands. They were gloved in white cotton, pristine and seamless, but there was a slight, rhythmic twitch in the waiter's left thumb.

"The secret," Sterling boomed, oblivious, "is knowing when to fold. Most men hold the card until it burns a hole in their pocket. I, however—"

Sterling took a deep, hearty swallow of the broth.

Vane stopped chewing his own meal. He noticed the shift instantly. Sterling didn't swallow again; instead, his throat hitched. The loud, booming voice vanished, replaced by a wet, clicking sound. 

Sterling paused. He frowned, tilting his head as if listening to a sound only he could hear. He tried to speak, but the words didn't come—only a thin, whistling gasp.

"Arthur?" Vane asked, his voice low and steady.

Sterling didn't answer. He reached for his water glass, but his hand began to tremble. It wasn't a shiver; it was a violent, systemic shudder. The glass tipped, sending a wave of sparkling water across the white linen cloth, but Sterling didn’t seem to notice. He was staring at Vane, his eyes widening, the pupils pinning into tiny black dots.

The tension in the room shifted. The other diners were still chatting, the clink of silver on porcelain continuing in a rhythmic, indifferent symphony. But in their small circle of candlelight, the air had turned electric.

Sterling suddenly lurched forward. He clawed at his collar, his face flushing a deep, bruised purple. He tried to stand, his chair screeching harshly against the parquet floor, drawing a few curious glances from the neighboring tables. 

Morel, the waiter, stepped forward. He didn't rush. He didn't gasp. He simply placed a hand on Sterling’s shoulder—not to steady him, but as if to guide him down.

"Is there a problem, Monsieur?" Morel asked. His voice was a flat, tonal void.

Sterling collapsed. He didn't fall gracefully; he hit the table first, his chest slamming into the edge, before sliding heavily to the floor. He spent his final seconds in a series of jagged, rhythmic spasms, his fingers drumming a frantic, senseless beat against the carpet.

As the dining room erupted into a blur of panicked voices and rushing staff, Vane didn't move. He remained seated, staring at the table.

His eyes locked onto the spilled water. 

The water had flowed across the linen, carving a path toward Sterling’s discarded spoon. In the clear liquid, a tiny, iridescent film had formed—a shimmering, oily swirl that didn't belong in a clear broth. 

But it wasn't the oil that caught Vane's attention. It was the spoon. 

As the water receded, Vane saw a single, crystalline grain of something white clinging to the underside of the silver bowl—not dissolved, but trapped in a tiny nick in the metal. 

Vane looked up. Morel was already retreating into the shadows of the kitchen doors, his expression as blank as a fresh sheet of paper. He hadn't looked at the body once. He had been looking at Vane.
